questions.q: What is the main practical difference between a managed package and an unlocked package, per this lesson?
options: They are functionally identical, just named differently
Unlocked packages can only be created through a packaging UI, never the CLI

A managed package is IP-protected and built for distributing a product externally (such as via AppExchange) with a structured upgrade path; an unlocked package has unlocked, inspectable metadata and is built for modular internal application development via Salesforce CLI
Managed packages cannot be upgraded once installed
questions.explain: Managed packages protect intellectual property for external distribution and support structured upgrades; unlocked packages leave metadata inspectable and modifiable, built through Salesforce CLI for internal, source-driven development.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend an unlocked package, rather than a managed package, for a typical internal application?
options: Because the business doesn't need IP protection from itself, and the source-driven, CLI-based workflow aligns better with a modern DX development process than the AppExchange-oriented managed package model
Because unlocked packages are always cheaper to license
Because managed packages cannot contain any custom objects
Because unlocked packages are required by Salesforce for any org with more than one application
questions.explain: An internal application doesn't need IP protection from its own organization, and unlocked packages' CLI-based, source-driven workflow fits an internal DX pipeline (version control, CI/CD, scratch orgs) better than the managed package model built for AppExchange distribution.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect packaging to Lesson 4's application boundary concept?
options: Packaging and application boundaries are unrelated concerns
Application boundaries can only be decided after packages already exist
Packaging eliminates the need to ever draw an application boundary

Packaging is the concrete Salesforce DX mechanism that turns a deliberate boundary decision into something enforced in version control, deployment, and dependency management -- rather than remaining purely conceptual
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames packaging as the enforcement mechanism for a boundary decision made using Lesson 4's signals -- the package has an explicit declared set of metadata, unlike an undifferentiated org.

questions.q: What real cost does this lesson say packaging introduces, which is why boundary decisions should be deliberate rather than reflexive?
options: Packaging has no real cost or overhead of any kind
Real process overhead: dependency management, package-version promotion, and more deliberate release coordination -- worth it for a genuinely separable application, not worth it otherwise
Packaging always requires purchasing additional Salesforce licenses
Packaging prevents any further development on the packaged metadata
questions.explain: The lesson names dependency management, version promotion, and release coordination as real overhead that packaging adds, which is exactly why Lesson 4 argued the underlying boundary decision needs to be deliberate rather than automatic.

questions.q: In this lesson's practical approach to deciding package boundaries for a multi-application org, what should happen with genuinely reusable components (per Lesson 10)?
options: Each application package should duplicate its own copy of the shared logic independently
Shared components should never be packaged at all
They should live in a shared, common utilities package that other application packages explicitly declare a dependency on, rather than being duplicated
Shared components must always go into a managed package regardless of audience
questions.explain: The lesson recommends a shared utilities package for genuinely reusable pieces, with explicit declared dependencies from the application packages that need them, instead of duplicating shared logic across every application package.
